title: What Happens Inside a Data Center

youtube.title: What Happens Inside a Data Center (Where the Internet Lives)
youtube.summary: Every photo, message and video you stream lives in a giant, windowless building full of computers. In this video we walk inside a data center: what happens when you tap play, what racks and servers are, how batteries and diesel generators keep the power on, why AI is pushing electricity use up so fast, and how hot aisles, cold aisles and liquid cooling fight the heat.
youtube.details:
Key facts (checked November 2026):
- Data centres used about 415 TWh in 2024, roughly 1.5% of global electricity; IEA projects about 945 TWh by 2030 (IEA Energy and AI, via Data Centre Magazine)
- Standard racks are 42U tall; 1U = 1.75 in (44.45 mm)
- Power path: grid, on-site substation, UPS batteries, diesel generators that start within seconds
- Nvidia H100 SXM: up to 700 W; an 8-GPU server draws around 10 kW
- Hot/cold aisle containment; liquid cooling with cold plates and immersion
- PUE: older sites around 2.0, industry average around 1.5, Google fleet around 1.1
- OVHcloud Strasbourg data center fire, March 2021

shorts.headline: Why AI needs so much power
Why data centers never lose power

scenes.sub: about 1.5% of all the world's electricity
scenes.text: Every photo you upload, every message you send and every video you stream ends up in the same kind of place. Not a cloud floating in the sky, but a huge, loud, windowless building packed with computers. These buildings are called data centers. In twenty twenty four, data centers around the world used about four hundred and fifteen terawatt hours of electricity. That is roughly one and a half percent of all the electricity used on Earth. And the International Energy Agency expects that number to more than double by twenty thirty. In this video we will walk inside one, and see how it handles your click, keeps its power on, and fights its biggest enemy, heat.

scenes.chapterTitle: From your tap to a server

items.text: Fibre carries it to a data center

scenes.text: Let us start with what happens when you tap play on a video. Your phone sends a small request through your mobile network or Wi-Fi, across fibre optic cables, to a data center, often the nearest one that has a copy of that video. Inside, a network switch passes the request to a server. The server finds the file on its drives and starts sending it back, piece by piece, along the same kind of path. All of this usually takes well under a second. You never see the building, but every time you scroll, search or stream, a computer somewhere is doing the work for you.

items.name: Racks
items.desc: Tall metal cabinets in long rows

scenes.text: Walk through the door, past the security checks, and you find long, cold rows of tall metal cabinets. These cabinets are called racks. Each rack holds a stack of flat computers called servers. A server is a lot like your laptop, but without a screen or keyboard, and usually with far more memory and processing power. At the top of each rack sits a network switch that connects every server to the rest of the building. Then there are the parts you do not see at first: thick power cables, huge cooling machines, and backup batteries. A large data center can hold tens of thousands of servers.

Racks are built to a standard size, so equipment from any company fits. A typical rack is forty two units tall. One unit is one point seven five inches, or about four and a half centimetres. A thin server might take just one unit, while a big AI server can take eight or more. Each server slides in on rails, like a drawer, and plugs into power and network cables at the back. Engineers can pull one out and replace it in minutes without switching off the rest. That is important, because in a building this big, some part is almost always being repaired.

items.text: Grid power arrives at high voltage

scenes.text: A data center can never simply lose power, so electricity follows a careful path. It arrives from the grid at very high voltage, and an on site substation steps it down. From there it flows through a U P S, which stands for uninterruptible power supply. A U P S is basically a giant bank of batteries. If the grid fails, the batteries take over instantly, without even a flicker. But batteries only last minutes. So within seconds, huge diesel generators start up and take over the load. Most sites also keep spare equipment, so if one part fails, another is ready. Engineers call this redundancy.

And the amount of power is growing fast, mostly because of AI. A typical laptop uses tens of watts. One of the popular AI chips used in data centers, Nvidia's H one hundred, can use up to seven hundred watts on its own. Put eight of them in one server, and that single machine can draw around ten kilowatts, as much as several homes. Now fill a whole rack, then a whole hall, with machines like that. This is why new AI data centers are planned in hundreds of megawatts, and why tech companies are signing deals for whole power plants. The hardest part is no longer the computers. It is the electricity.

Every watt that goes into a server comes out as heat. Without cooling, the room would overheat in minutes. So data centers are carefully arranged. Racks are placed in rows facing each other. Cold air is pushed into the aisle in front of the servers, called the cold aisle. Fans inside each server pull that cold air through, and blow the hot air out the back, into the hot aisle. Big cooling units then pull the hot air away, chill it, and send it back around. Keeping hot and cold air from mixing is one of the simplest ways to save energy, so many sites close off the aisles with doors and roofs.

items.title: Immersion
items.sub: in a liquid that doesn't conduct

scenes.text: But AI servers make so much heat that air alone is starting to struggle. Air is simply not very good at carrying heat away. Water is far better. So newer data centers use liquid cooling. In one method, called cold plates, metal blocks sit directly on top of the hottest chips, with cool liquid flowing through them. In another, called immersion cooling, entire servers are dunked in a special liquid that does not conduct electricity. The warmed water then travels to chillers or cooling towers outside, where the heat is released into the air. Some cities in Europe even pipe this waste heat into nearby homes.

So how do engineers know if a data center is efficient? They use a number called P U E, or power usage effectiveness. You take all the electricity the building uses and divide it by the electricity that actually reaches the computers. A perfect score would be one, meaning every watt goes into computing. An older data center might score around two, so half its power goes into cooling, lights and losses. The industry average today is roughly one point five. And the best large sites, like Google's, report a score of around one point one. Every drop in that number saves enormous amounts of energy and money.

Data centers are also built to survive almost anything. Many have two separate power feeds and two network connections, coming in from different directions. Your data is usually copied to several servers, and often to a second data center in another city or country, so one failure does not lose it. Physical security is serious too: fences, guards, cameras, key cards and sometimes fingerprint scanners. Still, accidents happen. In twenty twenty one, a fire destroyed one of OVHcloud's data center buildings in Strasbourg, France, and knocked many websites offline. That is exactly why companies keep copies in more than one place.

items.text: Your click travels to racks of servers
Batteries and generators back up the grid

scenes.text: Let us recap in three points. One. When you tap or click, your request travels over fibre to a building full of servers stacked in racks. Two. Power comes from the grid, with batteries and diesel generators ready to take over in seconds. Three. Nearly every watt turns into heat, so cooling, with air, water and liquid, is a huge part of the design. The cloud is not in the sky. It is in buildings like these, humming day and night.

scenes.title: Inside a data center
scenes.text: So the next time a video starts instantly, remember the giant, humming building somewhere that just did the work for you, with batteries, generators and a lot of cold air standing by. Now I want to hear from you. Did you think the cloud was something else? Tell me in the comments. If you enjoyed this, subscribe to Tech Explained. In the next video, we will find out how your phone's touchscreen knows exactly where your finger is.
